rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four passages progress from wine as provision (16:67), to mixed benefit and sin (2:219), avoiding prayer while drunk here, and finally complete prohibition (5:90).
rows.anchor: four verses address the consumption of wine or intoxicating drinks, and only one of them bans wine explicitly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jurisprudence treats 5:90 as the authoritative final ruling, based on Prophetic sayings and practice, abrogating the other passages’ legal implications.
rows.anchor: Islamic jurisprudence, basing itself upon Prophetic sayings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers must not approach prayer, its mosque, or prepare for it while drunk; they may do so once sober and able to understand their recitation.
rows.anchor: not to approach the prayer itself or the mosque(ṣalāh/ṣalawāt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣalāh or ṣalawāt can mean the place of prayer as well as prayer itself.
rows.anchor: ṣalāh/ṣalawāt, or “prayer(s),” can also connote the place of prayer; cf. 22:40

rows.speaker: Companions of the Prophet
rows.claim: A report says the verse followed Companions praying after drinking wine while drinking was still permitted and reciting a Quranic passage incorrectly.
rows.anchor: This part of the verse was reportedly revealed when some Companions of the Prophet attempted to pray after having drunk wine

rows.speaker: Muslims
rows.claim: After the verse, Muslims reportedly drank only after the evening prayer until wine was forbidden.
rows.anchor: Muslims would drink wine only after they had completed the evening prayer (ʿishāʾ)

rows.speaker: minority tradition
rows.claim: A minority tradition includes excessive sleepiness in drunkenness, since it impairs prayer; on this reading the verse was not wholly abrogated by the wine ban.
rows.anchor: A minority tradition extends the meaning of“drunkenness”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Junub means major ritual impurity and derives from a root meaning distance; the impure should keep distant from prayer and its places until purified, paralleling intoxication.
rows.anchor: Ritual impurity translates junub, which denotes major ritual impurity and derives from a root meaning to be distant from something

rows.speaker: legal scholars
rows.claim: Legal scholars hold that major ritual impurity also prohibits touching or reciting the Quran.
rows.anchor: According to legal scholars, the state of junub also prohibits one from touching or reciting the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Washing means completing major ritual ablution through full immersion, such as a bath or shower.
rows.anchor: Until you have washed refers to completing the major ritual ablution, which requires full immersion (as in a bath or shower)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception covers junub travelers seeking temporary shelter in a mosque and Companions whose adjacent homes required crossing the Prophet’s mosque to leave.
rows.anchor: An exception is made for those passing through, that is, travelers in a state of junub who need to seek shelter temporarily in a mosque

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Clean earth substitutes for water when illness prevents seeking or safely using water, or on a journey where water is unavailable.
rows.anchor: This verse also establishes an important easing of the rules of ritual purity by allowing the substitution of clean earth for water

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 5:6 gives nearly identical ritual-purity instructions.
rows.anchor: see also 5:6 for a nearly identical set of injunctions related to purity

rows.speaker: the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah
rows.claim: The verse reportedly followed ʿĀʾishah losing a necklace while traveling with the Prophet. The group camped to search, lacked water, complained they could not wash, and the verse came at dawn prayer.
rows.anchor: the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah lost a necklace while journeying with the Prophet and a group of Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ablution is called tayammum after the verse’s verb tayammamū, “resort to.”
rows.anchor: came to be known as tayammum, from the verb tayammamū

rows.speaker: a ḥadīth
rows.claim: A hadith lists God’s making dust purifying for Muslims among His blessings favoring them over other peoples.
rows.anchor: A ḥadīth refers to the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣaʿīd may mean high, hard, or rocky ground; ṭayyib may mean good, pure, or wholesome, leading some to suggest arable soil.
rows.anchor: The term used for earth

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says ṣaʿīd is any pure or clean part of the earth’s surface; dust adhering to the hands purifies.
rows.anchor: Al-Ṭabarī asserts that it refers to any pure or clean part of the surface of the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Precious metals and gems are unsuitable as clean earth for tayammum.
rows.anchor: Precious metals and gems are not suitable as sources of clean earth for the tayammum

rows.speaker: legal schools
rows.claim: Schools differ on water-search requirements, illness threshold, whether tayammum removes impurity or temporarily permits prayer, and whether prayer must be repeated if water is found before prayer time ends.
rows.anchor: There are differences among the legal schools as to whether the absence of water is a condition for the acceptability of the tayammum

rows.speaker: legal scholars
rows.claim: Scholars disagree whether “touching women” means intercourse only or any touch, regardless of desire.
rows.anchor: They also disagree about the extent to which one would have to “touch women” in order to become impure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tayammum requires intention, then two contacts with earth or stone: one to wipe the face, one to wipe the hands.
rows.anchor: make the niyyah or intention to perform the tayammum then to touch the earth or rub a piece of stone twice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some identify Madinan Jews, but the author considers the People of the Book generally the more likely referent.
rows.anchor: These verses continue the criticism of the Madinan Jews (Q) or more likely of the People of the Book in general (Z)

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators connect the purity claims to assertions that Jews or the People of the Book are God’s children and beloved, and alone entitled to Paradise.
rows.anchor: Most commentators see this as a reference to spiritual assertions the Jews or the People of the Book are said to make elsewhere in the Quran

rows.speaker: a group of Madinan Jews
rows.claim: Some say a group claimed to the Prophet that they were sinless, that daytime sins were forgiven at night, or that they could absolve one another through intercession; the Quran does not explicitly attest the claims.
rows.anchor: Some say that it refers to a group of Madinan Jews who approached the Prophet, claiming that they were free of sin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran warns everyone against considering themselves pure; God alone knows who is truly pure.
rows.anchor: The Quran warns people in general not to consider themselves pure (53:32). God alone knows those who are truly pure and those who are not

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatīl may be the date-stone thread or soil scraped between fingers, Quranic images of insignificance; here it means no one is wronged even slightly.
rows.anchor: The thread of a date stone renders fatīl, which might also mean the bit of soil that one can find by scraping between one’s fingers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 50 calls purity claims lies against God and a sin in themselves; claiming one’s own soul is pure is unacceptable in Islam.
rows.anchor: Such assertions of purity and sinlessness are said in v. 50 to be lies against God, a sin in itself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph models refusal to claim purity: exposed treachery leads him to say he does not absolve his own soul, which commands evil.
rows.anchor: Even the falsely accused prophet Joseph asserted, when the treachery of his would-be seductress was revealed, But I absolve not my own soul

rows.speaker: Sufis
rows.claim: Sufis warn that the carnal soul is not the locus of human purity.
rows.anchor: particularly odious to the Sufis, who warned that the carnal soul

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: Being pleased with one’s own soul extinguishes the lights of certitude.
rows.anchor: being pleased with one’s own soul extinguished the lights of certitude (Su)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Self-satisfaction is a source of disobedience and heedlessness.
rows.anchor: was the source of disobedience and heedlessness (Aj)

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: Anyone persuaded by praise of their purity or by their own self-estimation is veiled in ignorance.
rows.anchor: anyone who was persuaded by others’ high opinions of their purity or by their own high estimation of themselves was veiled in ignorance (Qu)

words: كُلَّمَا نَضِجَتْ جُلُودُهُم بَدَّلْنَٰهُمْ جُلُودًا غَيْرَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated consumption and replacement of Hell’s skins conveys punishment continuing without end.
rows.anchor: The image of the skins of those in Hell being consumed

words: كُلَّمَا نَضِجَتْ جُلُودُهُم بَدَّلْنَٰهُمْ جُلُودًا غَيْرَهَا
rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators take the Quran’s afterlife pleasures and torments literally rather than as metaphors for spiritual reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: understood by some commentators as suggesting that the pleasures and torments of the Afterlife as described in the Quran are meant to be taken literally

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Others read “skins” as garments of pitch worn in Hell; as they burn, they are replaced so the condemned can be set alight again.
rows.anchor: Others say that skins refers to the garments made of pitch (14:50) that those in Hell will wear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The renewal has also been understood as changing the attributes of those in Hell without changing their essence.
rows.anchor: The constant renewal of their skins has also been understood as indicating a continuous change in the attributes of those in Hell without any change in their essence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the fourth and final revelation on intoxicants: after 16:67, 2:219, and 4:43, it completely prohibits wine and gambling.
rows.anchor: This is the fourth and final passage in the chronological order of revelation relating to intoxicating drinks

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maysir names a specific pre-Islamic Arabian gambling game, but applies to all gambling; the wine ban extends to every intoxicant.
rows.anchor: Gambling translates maysir, a specific form of gambling popular in pre-Islamic Arabia

rows.speaker: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb
rows.claim: In a sermon, ʿUmar explained khamr, technically grape wine, as what clouds the intellect; thus the ban covers any mind-clouding substance.
rows.anchor: explained by ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb in a sermon in which he said

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition on intoxicants includes their sale and any profit from selling them.
rows.anchor: the ban on intoxicating beverages includes not only their consumption, but also their sale and any profit attained by it

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some extend the gambling ban to time-wasting games such as chess and backgammon; the author says neither was legally banned and both remain popular among Muslims.
rows.anchor: Some considered the ban on gambling to extend to all games that squander people’s time fruitlessly, such as chess and backgammon

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anṣāb likely refers to animal sacrifice at stone altars, a practice mentioned in 5:3 as making meat unlawful.
rows.anchor: is likely a reference to the idolatrous practice of sacrificing animals

rows.speaker: Companions of the Prophet
rows.claim: Accounts say the verse followed drunken Companions fighting, with one man seriously injured.
rows.anchor: Some accounts report that the present verse was revealed after some of the Prophet’s Companions became drunk and began to fight with one another

words: إِنَّمَا يُرِيدُ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنُ أَن يُوقِعَ بَيْنَكُمُ ٱلْعَدَٰوَةَ وَٱلْبَغْضَآءَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wine and gambling give Satan means to sow hostility among believers and distract from remembrance and prayer; similar hostility is assigned to Christians and Jews due to forgetfulness or disobedience.
rows.anchor: wine and gambling should be avoided, because they are a means through which Satan may cause enmity and hatred among the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers’ vain discussion of God’s signs aims to deny and deride them.
rows.anchor: The disbelievers engage in vain discussion about the signs of God, seeking to deny and deride them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran associates vain discussion with pejorative play, warns against taking religion as play or diversion, and commands avoidance of vain talk generally.
rows.anchor: The Quran links such vain discussion elsewhere with “playing” in a pejorative sense

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Religious and legal gossip can damage the community: false adultery accusations may cause miscarriages of justice, division, and mistrust.
rows.anchor: 24:14–16 indicates that vain discussion in matters of religion and law can have serious consequences for the community

words: فَأَعْرِضْ عَنْهُمْ حَتَّىٰ يَخُوضُوا۟ فِى حَدِيثٍ غَيْرِهِۦ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The counsel addresses the Prophet and all believers: withdraw from religious disparagement until the topic changes; other verses reinforce this.
rows.anchor: This verse thus counsels the Prophet, and by extension all believers, to avoid or remove themselves from groups engaged in vain discussion about religious matters

words: فَأَعْرِضْ عَنْهُمْ حَتَّىٰ يَخُوضُوا۟ فِى حَدِيثٍ غَيْرِهِۦ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One need only leave until the group moves to another topic.
rows.anchor: Here, one need only turn away from them until they move on to another topic

rows.speaker: some reports
rows.claim: Some reports connect the warning with 6:65’s factions, extending it to believers in fruitless, divisive religious debate.
rows.anchor: Some reports connect the warning in this verse regarding those

rows.speaker: some literalists
rows.claim: Some literalists read this as forbidding all religious discussion and debate and requiring reliance only on literal scripture.
rows.anchor: Some literalists have taken this verse to mean a prohibition against all discussion and debate regarding religious issues

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī rejects that reading: yakhūḍū means disrespectful, disparaging discussion, not sincere religious deliberation, which the Quran encourages.
rows.anchor: But al-Rāzī rejects such an interpretation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan may cause forgetfulness or make people miss when talk turns disparaging; once aware, they should leave.
rows.anchor: Satan may cause people to forget the prohibition against sitting among those engaged in vain discussion of religion

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: That Satan can cause the Prophet to forget raises difficult issues, though other verses indicate prophets can be subject to Satan’s whisperings.
rows.anchor: that he is capable of causing the Prophet to forget raises some difficult issues (Āl)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reckoning of disbelievers and those in vain discussion does not fall on the reverent; they are not judged by association, since none bears another’s burden.
rows.anchor: none bears the burden of another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers must remind, oppose, and exhort those in vain religious discussion, not merely leave them.
rows.anchor: believers should not only leave them, but also show their displeasure with and opposition to the discussion and exhort them against it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Splitting grain and fruit stones brings life from what appears dead, linking the cleavage to God bringing the living from the dead.
rows.anchor: That God is the Cleaver of the grain and the fruit stone is connected to His bringing forth the living from the dead

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The semantic link between splitting and creation also appears in al-Fāṭir, “Originator,” whose root means “to split.”
rows.anchor: The connection between “cleaving” or “splitting” and creating is also made semantically in the Divine Name al-Fāṭir, “the Originator,” which is derived from the root meaning “to split”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bringing the living from the dead refers to first human creation and resurrection after death.
rows.anchor: He brings forth the living from the dead both when He creates human beings the first time and when He brings them forth through resurrection after death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bringing the dead from the living refers to God causing death, the end of earthly life.
rows.anchor: He brings forth the dead from the living when He causes death, or the end of their earthly existence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cycle evokes Muḥyī, Giver of Life, and Mumīt, Bringer of Death.
rows.anchor: it is important to recall the two Divine Names Muḥyī (Giver of Life; 30:50; 41:39) and Mumīt (Bringer of Death)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The life-death cycles mean mabdaʾ (origin) and maʿād (return), transporting souls and all beings between this world and the next.
rows.anchor: the complementary movements of creation and resurrection, referred to in Islamic discourse as mabdaʾ (origin) and maʿād (return)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Created nature likewise cycles through life and death: a dead seed emerges from a living plant and a living plant from a dead seed.
rows.anchor: An analogous cycle of death and life is also seen in various ways in the created order
